implementation_notes: The canonical Python bulkhead is one ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=n) per dependency: a bounded worker set isolates a blocking dependency while callers hold futures. Its work queue is unbounded, so bound pending work with an explicit admission counter (threading.BoundedSemaphore) or check before submitting and fail fast with a distinct exception, and use result(timeout=...) as the per-call deadline. The classic hand-written pool is never needed - the stdlib executor is the pool - only the queue bound has to be added; for CPU-bound isolation use ProcessPoolExecutor instead.

variants.name: ThreadPoolExecutor per dependency with an explicit queue bound
variants.implementation_notes: The canonical Python bulkhead is one ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=n) per dependency: a bounded worker set isolates a blocking dependency while callers hold futures. Its work queue is unbounded, so bound pending work with an explicit admission counter (threading.BoundedSemaphore) or check before submitting and fail fast with a distinct exception, and use result(timeout=...) as the per-call deadline. The classic hand-written pool is never needed - the stdlib executor is the pool - only the queue bound has to be added; for CPU-bound isolation use ProcessPoolExecutor instead.
pitfalls: ThreadPoolExecutor queues without limit: max_workers bounds threads only, so an unbounded backlog still exhausts memory and latency.
Submitting into the same pool while holding a worker's result deadlocks once all workers are busy; never nest pool tasks.
Exceptions surface only on result(), so unobserved futures hide dependency failures and metrics.
Threads are OS threads; per-dependency pools multiply them, so size workers by the dependency's real concurrency budget.

variants.name: asyncio.Semaphore admission per dependency
variants.implementation_notes: In async Python the bulkhead is a permit counter bound to the running event loop: asyncio.Semaphore(n) per dependency, async with sem around the await, and asyncio.wait_for for the bounded wait; asyncio primitives are not thread-safe, so create the semaphore inside the loop. anyio.CapacityLimiter is the structured-concurrency equivalent and integrates with run_sync and to_thread. The classic thread pool is replaced by the loop's own scheduling; keep an executor only for calls that block.
variants.code_sketch:
db_slots = asyncio.Semaphore(8)          # create inside the running loop

async def query(sql):
    async with db_slots:                 # at most 8 in flight per dependency
        return await db.query(sql)
# bounded wait: await asyncio.wait_for(db_slots.acquire(), timeout=0.05)
pitfalls: asyncio primitives are loop-bound and not thread-safe; creating a semaphore at import time binds it to no running loop and can raise or misbehave.
Use async with or try/finally: a bare acquire without guaranteed release leaks a permit on cancellation.
A semaphore bounds concurrency, not queue length - waiting tasks accumulate, so add wait_for or a pending counter to reject.
Blocking calls inside the guarded section stall the whole loop; offload them with run_in_executor or anyio.to_thread.
ThreadPoolExecutor queues without limit: max_workers bounds threads only, so an unbounded backlog still exhausts memory and latency.
Submitting into the same pool while holding a worker's result deadlocks once all workers are busy; never nest pool tasks.
Exceptions surface only on result(), so unobserved futures hide dependency failures and metrics.
Threads are OS threads; per-dependency pools multiply them, so size workers by the dependency's real concurrency budget.
